lecons.html:
God wants to extend his kingdom on the earth. For this, he chose to make men work. It has always been God’s original plan: to have the visible creation under man’s control. Everything that touches the earth and its surroundings requires man’s intervention. God is a great king whose kingdom is established in the heavens. God destined man to be governor of the earth under the kingdom of God. This direction was lost when man sinned. Jesus Christ took it back for us by his redemptive work. Thus, the extension of the kingdom of God is set in motion. To continue, Christ destined the Church as his agency. But for reasons of order and good organization, he established ministries within the Church.

Ministry according to Christ is service and not lordship (Matt 23:11). Service is done below and not above. Whoever considers himself a minister of Christ must go down; he must become ever smaller. It is nevertheless a privilege to be a minister of Christ. Indeed, honors are attached to it (John 12:26). The minister does not make it his concern, but God honors the minister more and more according to his obedience. God also demands that all honor his ministers. There are two categories of ministry: the captives of Christ given to the Church and the functions of believers.

lecons.titre: The captives of Christ given to the Church
lecons.html:
Reference: Eph 4:8-13

Generally, people speak of the five ministries. We use the term “captives” because the biblical text says that Christ made them captive and then gave them to the Church. Christians called into these five departments of work in the kingdom have no choice. They do not choose to do it nor the opposite. They do not choose the timing, the periodicity, the size, the place, etc. either. They have no choice. They are slaves brought into the palace to occupy sacred posts. If they refuse, they will suffer for it all their lives (1 Cor 9:16-17). The ministry will become a shadow that will haunt the fleeing minister to the grave. Let Jonah run away, God will pursue him!

Whoever is in this kind of ministry must devote himself entirely. He cannot practice his profession unless he uses it as a temporary means to meet the needs of the ministry until the ministry is able to meet his own (Acts 8:1-5; 2 Cor 11:7-8). The pursuit of professional success is excluded from his life. He must seek in everything the success of his ministry. If this implies that he prospers in his professional career to create the conditions and inventions necessary for his ministry, he will do so. But for most of them, the master called them out of their profession to be at the service of the kingdom. There are believers whom Christ charges with professional and financial success to meet the needs of the Christian world. This is part of the functions of believers. We will come back to it.

The five captives are the government ministers of the Church. It is on individuals that God rests his Church. He takes care of replacing them when necessary. There is no ministry called apostleship, prophecy, evangelism, pastorate or doctorate (or whatever one wants to call it). Even though the words apostleship and prophecy appear in the Bible, they do not have the sense of an empty office for which a qualified person is sought to fill it. They have rather the sense of a grace or a mandate. One therefore cannot sufficiently train people to fix them in a ministry. It is the persons who constitute in themselves, by the decision and sovereign action of God, the ministry and the minister. As for the governance of his Kingdom on earth, God decided to trust men who will base themselves solely on his word, the Bible. The work of the captives of Christ consists of:

  • Training the other Christians for their ministry or function
  • Building up the body of Christ by bringing Christians to maturity in the truth of the word and the knowledge of God
  • Effectively fighting the invasion of sects and doctrines of demons

lecons.titre: The five captives and their job descriptions
lecons.html:
Each of the five captives of Christ has a different job description, but they complement one another. None of the ministries can do without the others and none can sufficiently replace the other. They have different functions involving different combinations of spiritual gifts. The functions of believers are also found in their lives. In fact, it is the presence of combinations of spiritual gifts or the manifestation of its functions that allows ministers to be recognized. Let us see with the word each office and its specifications.

The Apostle

He lays the foundation of the faith (1 Cor 3:6, 10). The Apostle is one sent by Christ with a special commission to one or more nations, peoples, etc. The Apostle is a builder, even a pioneer. His primary desire is to proclaim Christ in places not reached, but even more to make sure the converts remain in the faith. He watches over their spiritual and doctrinal balance. He works great signs and wonders. We can distinguish five types of apostles:

  • The great Apostle: Jesus Christ, the one sent by God
  • The apostles of the Lamb: the twelve who spread the good news. They were present with Jesus during the whole time of his earthly ministry. Their mission is unique and cannot be done or repeated by other people: they were the eyewitnesses of the resurrection of Jesus Christ
  • The foundational apostles: the apostles from the first Christian communities, those who helped lay the foundation of Christian doctrine, like Paul, Barnabas, James, Jude, etc.
  • The apostles of nations: those who came out from among the Jews to go and announce the Gospel to the Gentiles (nations other than the Jewish nation), like Paul. This has nothing to do with the apostles and prophets of nations today who become so when they begin to preach outside their nation or when they become influential in the whole nation
  • The apostles of continuity: those who currently hold apostolic ministries

One of the major signs of apostles today is the desire for structuring the Church, the mission of the Church’s stability, the resolution of thorny problems that fight against the Church. They play the role of fathers in communities, in a city, a nation, a region. Their ministry is accompanied by signs and miracles.

The abilities of an apostle generally encompass the four other ministries. But he in no way replaces them. He is like the thumb of the hand. Just as the thumb can touch all the other fingers without replacing them, the apostle can briefly operate in the departments of the other ministries. If an apostle freezes for a long time in the office of pastor, for example, his anointing risks going out, especially if he is already aware of his calling. In many cases, people received the confirmation of this ministry after having worked for some time in another ministry. The case of Paul is an example: he first worked at the church of Antioch for a year as a teacher before being brought by the Holy Spirit into his apostolic ministry.

The gifts of the Holy Spirit he manifests: gifts of power, gifts of revelation

Inherent function: presiding, governance, exhortation, teaching

The Prophet

He completes the work of the apostles by bringing deep revelations that further activate the faith of new converts and local churches (Acts 11:27-30; 15:32, 40-41). The prophets of the New Testament do not function as diviners, but rather confirm the revelations already received by believers in their spirit (1 John 2:27). In the exercise of their ministries, prophets must work in groups so that the revelations may be judged and confirmed (Acts 11:27-28; 13:1; 1 Cor 14:29-31).

Note that not all who prophesy are prophets in the sense presented. Whoever has the gift of prophecy prophesies, but he is not a prophet. Whoever has the function of prophecy prophesies, even with a greater ability than the one who has only the gift. Yet he is not a prophet, because his function generally remains within the framework of a community. A person can be a pastor and have the function of prophecy highly developed in him. He is not a prophet for all that.

The prophet has received a mandate. He is called by Christ and is at his disposal as a servant. Christ can send him where he wants according to need, like Agabus who often traveled to deliver a message. He can also become an assistant of an apostle in order to confirm his direction by precise revelations, as Silas was. The prophet knows in his heart that God called him to this ministry. He does not suppose it on the basis of a few manifestations. This is, moreover, the case with all five government ministries of the Church.

The gifts of the Holy Spirit he manifests: gifts of revelation, vocal gifts, mainly prophecy

Inherent function: prophecy, exhortation (Acts 15:32)

The Evangelist

He is a proclaimer of the good news. He has a great desire to bring people to receive Christ as Lord and Savior. He is always ready to cry out what Christ did for the salvation of the whole world. The evangelist does not intervene in the government of the Church. His place is outside. He does not teach the Church. He has neither the time nor the ability. He is sent to announce to the lost world that everything is ready and that it can come home. He is the voice of the Church to the world. Every minister of God can occasionally do the work of an evangelist. The work of the evangelist must be completed by the apostles and followed by the pastors, otherwise the fruits may be lost. Evangelists stand out from Christians who have the Christian ministry of exhortation in that their works are accompanied by miracles. These are the evangelists whom the Apostle designates as those who have the gift of miracles (1 Cor 12:28).

The evangelist can train Christians to evangelize. He also leads the band. He is the leader of the conquest team, the Conqueror.

The gifts of the Holy Spirit he manifests: gifts of power, prophecy

Inherent function: exhortation, teaching

The Pastor

He is the shepherd (Eph 4:11; John 10:11-16). He is leader of the local Church. In the Bible, they are called elders or overseers. The overseers seem to be leaders of the college of elders (Titus 1:5, 7; 1 Tim 3:1-2; 5:17; Acts 20:17, 28). A pastor is often noticed with the following qualities:

  • He takes care of Christians by watching over their provision, protection and spiritual health
  • He is more and more watchful to take charge of others, especially the weak
  • People are drawn to him to confide, to get advice, support
  • He has a high spirit of listening
  • He is willing to help and to teach everyone
  • He loves the company of other children of God; he likes being in a group with other believers
  • He makes contact easily
  • His desire to serve God and others is not based on social considerations or a reward; his only aim is to do good and to please God
  • He gives of his own subsistence to help others stay firm in the faith despite trials

The apostle Paul speaks of pastors as those who have the gifts of healing, helping, governing, speaking various kinds of tongues (1 Cor 12:28).

The gifts of the Holy Spirit he manifests: vocal gifts (1 Cor 14:26-31, 39)

Inherent function: teaching, administration, healing by the prayer of faith according to James, familiarity with the nine functions of believers

The Teacher

This minister is busy bringing the Church to maturity through in-depth teaching of the ways of God (Acts 11:26; 13:1; 19:9-12; Luke 5:1; 6:17-19; 21:33). He has a mastery of the doctrines of Christianity that studies alone cannot justify. He probes the Scriptures in a particular and in-depth way. The teacher dissects the word, makes it tasty to the palate as a good restaurateur would. He lets believers grow in the deep knowledge of the word of God. A teacher is a man of God who has the ability to communicate knowledge in an easy-to-understand way. The teacher has the task of making the Scriptures crystal clear. He is like a puzzle specialist, able to quickly turn questions and uncertainties into understanding through the light of the Scriptures.

The gifts of the Holy Spirit he manifests: discerning of spirits, prophecy

Inherent function: exhortation, teaching

References: Rom 12:6-8; 1 Cor 12:28-30

The five captives of Christ work for the building up of the Body of Christ by bringing people to Christ and rooting them in the Word of God. But they do not work alone. It is the whole body of Christ that works and builds itself up. The five captive ministers train and equip the saints so that they are effective in their services for Christ. These services of believers are subdivisions of the duties of the captives that Christ places on the other members of his body. For example, a prophet prophesies, exhorts, brings revelations, etc. But not all who prophesy are prophets. There are people who exhort without being prophets or evangelists. We can call these workers of prophecy or of exhortation.

“having gifts differing according to the grace that was given to us: if prophecy, let’s prophesy according to the proportion of our faith; or service, let’s give ourselves to service; or he who teaches, to his teaching; or he who exhorts, to his exhorting; he who gives, let him do it with generosity; he who rules, with diligence; he who shows mercy, with cheerfulness.” (Rom 12:6-8)

God has set some in the assembly: first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracle workers, then gifts of healings, helps, governments, and various kinds of languages. (1 Cor 12:28)

Prophecy

Whoever has this function is under obligation to prophesy whenever the need arises. It is a burden imposed on him. He is under obligation to console and exhort the people. He takes the initiative of prophecy. The function of prophecy goes beyond the gift of prophecy. Whoever has the gift only will always wait for the Holy Spirit to decide when and where to prophesy. Whoever is a worker of prophecy decides when and where to use the gift of prophecy. He then prays and obtains the anointing for the work at the precise moment (2 Kings 3:15-16). That is why he is called to operate by the proportion of faith (Matt 7:7; Mark 11:24; 1 John 5:14-15). This function must be developed just as one grows in faith. The whole Church must aspire to this function (1 Cor 14:24; 1 Peter 4:11).

The Deacon (Server)

Diakonia means servant, someone who carries out another’s orders. The word can be used to speak of anyone in God’s service, even the five government ministries. This is the framework that lets us distinguish the function of deacons and deaconesses. They mainly take care of service at the table, that is, social aid. They are also in charge of paperwork and logistics. They are not necessarily in control of finances, but they watch over the good management of financial and material resources. Their insight and accounting awareness help avoid in the Church presumptuous moves, fruitless investments and misuse of available resources (Acts 6:1-5; 1 Tim 3:8-13; 1 Cor 4:2).

Teaching

It is the ability to faithfully pass on to others what one has received as teaching, so as to build up people in the local Church (2 Tim 2:2; Heb 5:12). Example: Priscilla and Aquila received the teaching of the apostle Paul. They passed it on to Apollos who continued (Acts 18:24-28).

Exhortation

The ability to call another person to follow oneself and to lead him where he should go. Whoever has this function has the burden of seeing others draw near to God. There are four branches in this service:

a) Soul winners

With a burden for the unconverted, he finds it easy to encourage them to give themselves to Christ (John 1:40-46). The soul winner resembles an evangelist a little. But he is not one, simply because his ministry, although it draws many people to Christ, is not accompanied by miracles. It was Christians in the soul-winning ministry who started the church of Antioch before the apostle Barnabas came to lay the foundations (Acts 11:19-26). Moreover, when Barnabas arrived at Antioch, he was not yet an apostle. He was, as his name means, Son of Encouragement (exhortation). This ministry was so dominant in his life that the apostles changed his name to it (Acts 4:36).

b) Encourager

Encourages Christians in the right way (Acts 9:26-27; 11:22-26).

c) Worship and praise leader

This is not only someone who has musical talents. Whoever has the gift of the Holy Spirit to lead praise has an anointing. When he starts to sing, even without a musical instrument, people are quickly in the spirit. Elisha needed it to activate his own anointing (2 Kings 3:15).

Whoever has this function in the Church must not only know songs; he must be filled with the Word of God and the Holy Spirit (Eph 5:18-19; Col 3:16).

d) Intercessor

Praying for someone is a kind of spiritual exhortation. It calls the person to the will of God (Col 4:12). It is a way of being with a person (Rom 15:30), of going ahead to prepare the way for him (Luke 22:31-32).

Giving (the one who gives)

This is generosity inspired by the Holy Spirit. Whoever has this function wants to share what he has with others. He has in him an ever-growing desire to share. Also, he gives without restraint. What he must do is direct his work primarily in the house of God. He must aim at the harvest, the servants of God and the children of God in need (Gal 6:9-10). God generally gives such people an ease in undertaking and making money. This is to give them the resources for the ministry. His professional and financial success is meant to meet the needs of the Christian world. He must avoid hesitating or disobeying the direction of the Holy Spirit. He must not follow his feelings and must not let himself be guided by men. He is a steward of the goods entrusted to him. He must distribute as God wants.

Leadership (the one who presides)

This is the management, organization and structuring of things. It is superintendence. The overseers and elders lead (preside over) the Church. The same word is used (1 Tim 3:4-5; 1 Tim 5:17). Thus, this can be another word for elder or overseer. This is the one who can be placed at the head of the organization to structure things, distribute tasks and follow the progress of the project. He sees a bigger picture and cannot be too much in the details.

The Governor (the team leader)

Whoever has this charisma is a leader, a group driver who is more focused on people’s needs than on paperwork and logistics. He is a team leader who wants his teammates to do well and to produce properly without stress. He can bring people to do things without their feeling the pressure. He has an objective that he pursues while loving his people.

The Helps (assistance)

The people who accompany men of God and assist them. They can help baptize new converts, be sent by ministers to places they cannot immediately take care of, or to any other affairs of the kingdom under the direction of the man of God (Rom 16:3, 9; see also Num 11:17). These are subordinate ministers who are closer to the man of God and carry his burden with him. The Levites are called by the Talmudists helpers of the priests.

Mercy

This is the service rendered to the needy. This person easily feels the pains of others. He goes beyond physical needs. He does not always have the means to do what his holy feelings demand. His solution is in prayer. If he intervenes before God with this mercy, he can obtain forgiveness, healing, deliverance, salvation and all kinds of solutions for others. Generally, God uses him to act when he prays. That is, he finds himself, without forcing himself, being the answer to his own prayer. He can also take quick actions according to the means at his disposal. In any case, if he steps into a matter, everything yields to him, even God. There is no situation that resists him. Mercy triumphs over judgment (James 2:13).

Other services

We have cited only the prominent services. There are of course many others. Moreover, the Lord can turn into a ministry for someone any gift the Holy Spirit has given him. For example, the apostle in verse 28 of chapter 12 of his first letter to the Corinthians cites the ministries (apostles, prophets, teachers) and continues with “… then miracle workers, then gifts of healings … and various kinds of languages” (1 Cor 12:28). This means that, for these, the gift has risen to the level of a ministry. It is their work from then on. If healing is needed somewhere and he is in the area, it will be enough to call him. He will simply heal the person. The same goes for working of miracles, speaking in tongues and interpretation of tongues.

You must know it in order to fulfill it well (Col 4:17).

How to know your ministry?

  • Ask God (Matt 7:7; Jer 33:3)
  • Every ministry, whatever its size, shape and direction, is a matter of divine mandate. The minister must hear God speak. The way he hears it does not matter. But the minister must have the assurance of having received God’s call.
  • See the links of the gifts
  • The presence in your life of all the gifts of one of the five ministries is a clear sign of a call to that ministry. The regularity of the gift of prophecy is a sign of a call to the function of prophecy, etc.
  • See the motivations of the heart
  • A great passion to see people come to Christ is a sign of a call to the ministry of evangelist or at least to the function of exhorter. A person who has the burden to pray for people, without being asked, has the function of exhorter (he is an intercessor).
  • Consider the means available and professional abilities
  • No Christian is rich to live in opulence. God has his mission in view. Think about it and pray. If you are financially provided for, you are probably called to mercy or more exactly to giving. Your political, economic and professional position is a post from which Christ wants to see you act for the interest of his kingdom.
  • The needs of the field
  • If the needs of people in your immediate or wider environment make your heart and nerves burn, you are called to do something about it. Do not stay quiet, do not show indifference and do not be afraid. If you make decisions out of love for God, you can count on his protection, his provision and his direction. God is love.
  • Dreams, visions, audible voices
  • These are among many other spectacular means by which God calls. But often, they come as confirmation or to signal the urgency of the call, unless it is a father’s cry over a stubborn child.
  • Confirmation by a third party
  • Another person confirms what the called one has already received in his heart. No one should teach you your call. They only have the privilege of confirming it (Acts 13:1-3).

References: Col 4:17; Col 3:23-24; Col 3:17

“Man of God” is the title we want to bear and that is given to us. Is it with reason? Of course! We work with God who himself designates thus those who are at work for him. We are men and women of God. But then, we have an inner goal to reach. We must be complete and equipped for every good work. We must be well adjusted in order to be good examples.

We must work on ourselves to become ever more commendable so that the name of Christ may be glorified. This is what the apostle practiced all his life and what he exhorts us to do (Phil 3:12-14; 1 Cor 9:24-27).

How to get there?

By living each day by the Word of God. Confessing and declaring every moment the promises of Christ’s Covenant over our lives, situations and circumstances. Looking each day into the instructions and recommendations of the Word to make sure that we walk well in the steps of Christ and that we do not harm the men for whom he sacrificed himself. The whole Bible is our mirror. But certain texts are characteristic for men of God:

1 Tim 3:1-15, 1 Tim 4:12-16, 1 Tim 5:1-2, 1 Tim 5:19-22, 1 Tim 6:9-14, 1 Tim 6:20-21, 2 Tim 2:14-16, 2 Tim 2:22-25, 2 Tim 3:14-17, Titus 1:6-9, Titus 2:1, Titus 3:1-3, Titus 3:9-11

objectifs: ✦  You understand that every believer has a ministry — not only pastors.
✦  You know the five captives of Christ and you can identify them in your Church.
✦  You have identified your own function in the Body of Christ.
✦  You live ministerial ethics: exemplary conduct, humility, service.
✦  You serve concretely according to your grace without waiting for an official position.

qcm.q: What is God’s original plan, according to the introduction of the module?
c: To govern the earth without man
To have the visible creation under man’s control, who governs under his authority
To leave the earth without authority
To remove man from the earth
qcm.e: Christ gave back this mandate and entrusted to the Church the continuation of his work.

qcm.q: Why do we speak of the “captives” of Christ?
c: Because Christ made them captive and gave them to the Church: they have no choice to accept or refuse the call
Because they are prisoners of the law
qcm.e: Ephesians 4:8-13. Refusing this call means suffering all your life.

qcm.q: What are the five captives of Christ?
qcm.e: Five departments of work in the kingdom.

qcm.q: What is the common work of the five captives?
c: Training and equipping the saints for the building up of the body of Christ
qcm.e: The captives do not work alone: the whole body takes part.

qcm.q: What does the apostle do, according to the module?
c: He only handles the Church’s accounting
He lays the foundation of the faith, proclaims Christ where he is not known and watches that the converts remain in the faith
He teaches believers the ways of God in depth
He confirms the prophecies of others
qcm.e: 1 Corinthians 3:6, 10. The apostle is a builder, a pioneer, sent by Christ with a special commission.

qcm.q: What difference does the module make between the gift of prophecy and the ministry of prophet?
c: The prophet is a diviner who predicts the future
Whoever has the gift of prophecy prophesies without being a prophet; prophets work in groups so that revelations are judged
qcm.e: The prophets of the New Testament are not diviners: they confirm the revelations already received by believers (1 John 2:27; 1 Corinthians 14:29-31).

qcm.q: What does the module say about the evangelist?
c: He proclaims the Good News, often accompanied by miracles: he is the voice of the Church to the world
qcm.e: He does not intervene in the government of the Church.

c: The shepherd, leader of the local Church, who takes care of Christians

qcm.q: How many functions of believers does the module present (Romans 12:6-8; 1 Corinthians 12:28-30)?
qcm.e: Prophecy, deacon, teaching, exhortation, giving, leadership, governor, helps, mercy.

qcm.q: What does the role of the deacon (the server) consist of?
c: Service at the table: social aid, logistics and the good management of resources
qcm.e: Diakonia means servant: someone who carries out another’s orders.

qcm.q: What are the four branches of exhortation?
c: Soul winners, encouragers, worship leaders, intercessors
qcm.e: Calling a person and leading him where he should go.

qcm.q: What does Colossians 4:17 say about your ministry?
c: You must know it in order to fulfill it well
You must wait for it without doing anything
qcm.e: “Take heed to the ministry which you have received in the Lord, that you may fulfill it.”

qcm.q: What is the first step to know your ministry?
c: Wait for a pastor to say it
qcm.e: The minister must hear God speak, in one way or another.

qcm.q: Who confirms your call, according to the module?
c: Others have the privilege of confirming what you have already received: no one should teach you your call

qcm.q: What is the principle of ministry according to Christ (Matthew 23:11)?
qcm.e: The greatest among you will be your servant.

exercices.titre: Ministry test: my function in the body of Christ
exercices.consigne: For each statement, choose the number that best matches you.
exercices.intro_html:
This series contains 60 statements, and that is intentional. Your ministry is often hidden in reflexes you no longer notice: what you do without effort, what weighs on your heart, what others turn to you for when they need something. The more honestly you answer each statement, the more precise the portrait will be.

You have nothing else to do but choose a number. Answer quickly, without looking for the “right” answer. The statements are deliberately mixed: do not try to guess which function they relate to.

At the end, the application calculates your scores and shows you the functions that stand out most in your life, with advice to develop them.

items: I persevere in prayer for a person or a cause, even long after others have given up.
I am filled with the Word of God and the Holy Spirit, not only musically gifted.
I sometimes find myself being the answer to my own prayer for someone.
I actively look for opportunities to share the Gospel, even when no one asks me to.
I am naturally asked to lead a time of worship or praise.
I feel deep joy every time someone is converted through my testimony.
People often ask me to re-explain what they did not understand.
I easily and deeply feel the pain of others, even when they do not express it.
I am ready to carry a burden or a mission that the leader cannot take on alone right away.
I am naturally entrusted with structuring or organizing a collective project.
I feel close to God’s servants and I like to lighten their load in concrete ways.
I have the natural ability to encourage Christians to persevere in the right way.
I am easily entrusted with a responsibility related to managing resources or equipment.
When this burden arises, I take the initiative to act rather than wait to be asked.
When I sing or lead a time of praise, a particular anointing is manifested, even without an instrument.
God seems to give me a particular ease in undertaking or earning money.
I know how to distribute tasks and follow their progress without losing the thread.
My words often give courage and hope back to those who doubt.
People naturally follow me when I lead a group, without my needing to impose my authority.
I feel a particular weight to pray for specific people, regularly, without being forced.
People turn to me to give clear direction to a group or an activity.
I easily retain what I am taught and I am keen to pass it on faithfully to others.
This burden grows in me over time, like something that develops by faith.
I easily manage to steer a conversation toward Christ, without it being forced.
People feel stronger after talking with me.
I take care to remain faithful to what I received, without adding my own ideas.
Praying for someone seems to me a concrete way of walking with them in their struggle.
People often agree to give themselves to Christ after talking with me.
I clearly sense when the Holy Spirit urges me to give to someone or to a specific work, and I obey.
I am naturally attentive to the practical and logistical organization of an event or a service.
I often prefer to be in discreet support rather than on the front stage.
I am inclined toward the well-being of the people I lead, more than toward performance alone.
I know how to recognize the precise moment when I must speak, without confusing it with my own opinion.
I feel that leading praise activates something greater in me and in the assembly.
When I give, I do so without restraint, without expecting anything in return.
Taking care of material details (meals, room, resources) does not weigh on me, it motivates me.
I have a clear goal that I pursue, while staying attentive to each person on my team.
I feel comfortable supervising several people or several tasks at the same time.
I act quickly and concretely, with the means I have, as soon as I see a suffering to relieve.
I like preparing structured content to help someone grow in a biblical truth.
I know how to bring a team forward without putting people under pressure.
When I cannot act concretely for someone in need, I naturally turn to prayer.
God often shows me, during prayer, specific things about the people I intercede for.
I often feel a pressing burden to pass on a word of exhortation or consolation to someone.
People quickly enter the presence of God when I lead worship.
I quickly notice when someone is discouraged, even if they do not say so.
The people I lead feel loved and supported, not only directed.
My words often bring comfort or correction at the exact moment the person needed it.
I am drawn to the needy, the sick, people in suffering, more than to other forms of service.
I take the initiative to prepare the way through prayer even before a situation arises.
I quickly notice waste or misuse of resources and I seek to correct it.
I can be counted on to represent or carry out a delegated task faithfully.
I have a particular burden for people who do not yet know Christ.
I consider myself a steward of the goods God has entrusted to me, not their owner.
Serving “at the table”, in the shadows and without visible recognition, does not bother me.
I easily see the overall plan of a project, more than the small details.
I take the initiative to go to someone to lift them up, without waiting for them to ask.
I notice when what I passed on has really been understood and put into practice by someone.
I have a growing and natural desire to share what I have with others, beyond my obligations.
I feel comfortable accompanying and assisting a man or woman of God in his ministry.
champs.legende: 1 = not really me · 2 = sometimes, it depends · 3 = very often me

groupes.cours: It is an imposed burden: exhorting and consoling. Whoever has this function takes the initiative, prays, obtains the anointing at the precise moment and speaks according to the proportion of faith. It grows as one grows in faith.
steps: When the burden arises, pray first to receive the anointing (2 Kings 3:15-16), then speak.
Test every word against the Word of God, with humility (1 Corinthians 14:29).
Learn to distinguish your opinion from the burden of the Spirit: reread the 3 voices of module 6.
Practice in a small group or with your partner, and ask for honest feedback.

groupes.cours: The deacon (diakonia, servant) takes care of service at the table, that is, social aid, paperwork and logistics. He watches over the good management of material and financial resources and avoids waste.
steps: Offer yourself to the welcome, logistics or social aid team of your Church.
Be faithful in small things: inventory, cash, equipment (1 Corinthians 4:2).
Cultivate transparency: write things down, give an account, keep everything in order.
Train in management and organization (module 11 helps you with this).

groupes.cours: It is the ability to faithfully pass on what you received, to build up people in the local Church, like Priscilla and Aquila with Apollos.
steps: Choose a truth from the manual and teach it to one person, with a simple plan.
Check that the person understood and puts it into practice.
Stay faithful to what you received: do not add your own ideas (2 Timothy 2:2).
Dig into your subjects in depth (Hebrews 5:12) and look for a mentor.

groupes.cours: The soul winner has a burden for the unconverted and easily brings people to give themselves to Christ. He resembles an evangelist, without the miracles. It was they who started the church of Antioch.
steps: Share the Gospel every week: take up the assignments of module 9 again.
Keep a notebook of people, and pray for each name.
Accompany new converts in their first steps.
Work on your testimony and the plan of salvation (John 1:40-46).

groupes.cours: The encourager helps Christians stay in the right way, like Barnabas, “Son of Encouragement”.
steps: Each day, contact a discouraged person: a message, a call, a visit.
Learn to listen before speaking.
Keep confidential what is entrusted to you.
Always base your words on the Word of God (Acts 9:26-27; 11:22-26).

groupes.cours: The worship leader has an anointing: even without an instrument, people quickly enter the spirit. Knowing songs is not enough: you must be filled with the Word of God and the Holy Spirit.
steps: Feed your personal life with the Word and prayer before leading others (Ephesians 5:18-19; Colossians 3:16).
Sometimes sing without an instrument to recognize the anointing.
Join your Church’s praise team and serve under the direction of the leader.
Stay humble: music is a tool, the presence of God is the goal.

groupes.cours: Praying for someone is a spiritual exhortation: the intercessor walks with the person in their struggle and prepares the way for them.
steps: Keep an intercession journal (take up the one from module 7).
Set a regular hour to pray for specific names.
Practice the prayer of agreement with a partner.
Note what God shows you and the answers received (Colossians 4:12; Luke 22:31-32).

groupes.cours: Giving is generosity inspired by the Holy Spirit. God often gives these people an ease in undertaking and earning money, so that they may feed the work. They are stewards.
steps: Obey right away when the Spirit urges you to give, without following your feelings or men.
Direct your giving first toward the house of God, the servants of God and the children of God in need (Galatians 6:9-10).
Undertake with wisdom: module 11 on money and the creation of wealth will help you.
Remain a steward: everything comes from God and returns to God.

groupes.cours: Leadership is management, organization and structuring: placing someone at the head of a project to distribute tasks and follow progress. He sees the overall plan.
steps: Ask for the responsibility of a small project in your Church or your neighborhood.
Learn to plan, to divide tasks and to follow progress.
Keep your household in order: it is the school of leadership (1 Timothy 3:4-5).
Surround yourself with people who like details, and give an account.

groupes.cours: The governor is a team leader focused on people’s needs. He moves the group forward without pressure, with a clear objective, loving his people.
steps: Listen to each member of your team before deciding.
Set a clear objective and share it.
Encourage rather than press; correct gently.
Practice in a small group (cell, service team), then ask for feedback (1 Corinthians 12:28).

groupes.cours: Helps accompany men of God and carry their burden: baptizing, representing, assisting, going where the leader cannot go. They are subordinate ministers close to the man of God.
steps: Get close to a leader and offer regular help.
Faithfully carry out each delegated task, and give an account.
Stay discreet and loyal: discreet support is your strength.
Learn from him as Joshua from Moses (Romans 16:3, 9; Numbers 11:17).

groupes.cours: Mercy is the service rendered to the needy. Whoever has it easily feels the pain of others, prays when he cannot act, and often finds himself the answer to his own prayer. Mercy triumphs over judgment.
steps: Regularly visit the sick or people in difficulty, according to your means.
Turn each suffering into a subject for prayer, then for quick action.
Work with the social team (diaconate) of your Church.
Protect yourself from exhaustion: you are not the savior of everyone (James 2:13).
